title: UK Officials Said AI Would Add £400 Billion to the Economy. That Figure Mainly Came From Google
gist: The UK government repeatedly cited a £400 billion AI economic boost that came from a 2023 Google-commissioned report, while its own central estimate is £120 billion (range £55-140 billion) by 2030. The AI minister conceded this in a parliamentary answer without withdrawing the headline figure.

insights.claim: The UK government told the public AI could add £400 billion ($538 billion) to the economy, a figure meant to calm fears of job losses and an economic crash.
insights.speaker: Ben Gartside
insights.so_what: AI-upside narratives are used politically to offset displacement fears.

insights.claim: AI minister Kanishka Narayan said AI adoption and data investment could add £55-140 billion by 2030, with a central estimate of £120 billion, which he called hugely uncertain.
insights.speaker: Ben Gartside
insights.so_what: Official AI productivity expectations are under a third of the headline figure.

insights.claim: The £400 billion figure came from a 2023 report commissioned by Google and produced by Public First (now PF Global).
insights.speaker: Ben Gartside
insights.so_what: Industry-funded research drove government messaging and policy.

insights.claim: Departments used Google's figure for almost two years under two governments; ministers had the lower estimate since at least November 2025, yet Skills England still published the old figure four months later.
insights.speaker: Ben Gartside

insights.claim: The ministerial answer did not withdraw the £400 billion figure or say it was wrong, and is the first recorded instance WIRED found of the two numbers being set side by side.
insights.speaker: Ben Gartside
insights.so_what: The government hedges instead of correcting.

insights.claim: PF Global says the gap stems partly from assumptions of slower government AI adoption than were possible in 2023, and its central estimate for 2030 is now much closer to the government's, with growth ramping up after that.
insights.speaker: Ben Gartside
insights.so_what: Even the author of the original number now sees slower realization of AI gains near term.
insights.quote: assume a much slower rate of adoption than looked possible back in our model that was created in 2023

insights.claim: PF Global says its work for Google continues and that all research was independent.
insights.speaker: Ben Gartside

insights.claim: Commons committee chair Chi Onwurah said hype is one of the central barriers to digital transformation of public services, and overstating technology benefits undermines the case for change.
insights.speaker: Chi Onwurah
insights.so_what: Scrutiny of AI-driven public-sector savings claims is rising.

insights.claim: The Ada Lovelace Institute's Sumedha Deshmukh says precise-looking AI figures often embed assumptions and incentives, and industry often funds the research behind them; government should ask where a number came from, what it assumes and who benefits.
insights.speaker: Sumedha Deshmukh
insights.so_what: A useful skepticism checklist for AI-economics claims.
insights.quote: where did it come from, what does it assume, and who actually benefits from a given figure?

insights.claim: Lord Holmes said billions of pounds of public money depend on robust data, and that the government should have clarified the figure much sooner after he asked in January 2025 and got no answer.
insights.speaker: Lord Holmes of Richmond
insights.so_what: Public spending decisions may rest on inflated AI projections.

insights.claim: Former technology minister Peter Kyle also used the £400 billion figure while promoting AI, part of a wider debate over government support versus boosterism.
insights.speaker: Ben Gartside
insights.so_what: Policy tailwinds for AI may be rooted in optimistic figures.
